summary: Provides a lexicography for interpreting GMPLS terminology within the ITU-T's Automatically Switched Optical Network architecture. The definitions are not exclusive or complete, and GMPLS applies more widely than ASON. The document is informational.

eli5.summary: A dictionary that translates one group's technical words into the other group's words so they can work together.

questions: what is a te link in ason
how do ason and gmpls differ
subtitle: Translating GMPLS concepts into ASON architecture terminology

tldr.problem: GMPLS (IETF) and ASON (ITU-T) are two different architectures for controlling optical networks, and they use different terminology for similar concepts, making it hard for engineers to understand both.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a lexicography—a detailed translation dictionary—that maps GMPLS terms and concepts into the ASON context, showing what each GMPLS term means when applied to ASON networks.
tldr.outcome: Engineers familiar with ASON can read GMPLS specifications and understand the technical content by translating terms on the fly; the document enables both communities to work together.

facts.label: Primary focus
facts.value: Optical networks and traffic engineering control

today: RFC 4397 remains the authoritative reference for translating between GMPLS and ASON terminology, particularly for engineers working on optical network control. It has not been obsoleted, and the lexicography it provides continues to support collaboration between IETF and ITU-T standards bodies.

sections.title: Why Translation Matters
sections.content:
GMPLS (Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching) was developed by the IETF as a general framework for establishing labeled paths through many types of networks: packet networks (PSC), Layer 2 networks (Ethernet, ATM), time-division multiplex (TDM) networks, optical wavelength networks (LSC), and fiber-switching networks (FSC). ASON (Automatically Switched Optical Networks) was developed by the ITU-T specifically for controlling large-scale optical networks.

Both technologies aim to automate network control, but they come from different traditions: GMPLS from the Internet world, ASON from the telecommunications world. Each uses its own terminology, inherited from decades of work in their respective communities. This RFC is informational: it does not propose new technology or change either system. Instead, it teaches the terminology mapping so that engineers can understand documents written in either framework when applied to optical networks.
sections.eli5: Two different groups invented two different systems for automatically managing big optical networks. They use different words, so this document translates between them so they can understand each other.

sections.title: Fundamental Concepts and Sources
sections.content:
GMPLS terminology comes primarily from RFC 3945 and related RFCs (4201, 4202, 4204, 4206). ASON terminology comes from ITU-T recommendations (G.8080, G.8081, G.7713, G.7714, G.7715). Both are rich and detailed, and the reader must be familiar with the core documents before using this lexicography.

A key observation: in GMPLS, terminology distinguishes the data plane (where actual traffic flows) from the control plane (where control messages are sent and routing decisions are made). ASON also makes this distinction, using transport plane instead of data plane. Throughout this lexicography, angle brackets (e.g., <Data Plane>) mark the context in which a term applies.
sections.eli5: Both systems have documents that define their terms. This RFC takes those terms and shows how they correspond to each other.

sections.title: Network Entities and Components
sections.content:
In GMPLS, a transport node is a device that switches or routes data. A controller is the control-plane intelligence that manages one or more transport nodes. A Label Switching Router (LSR) combines a transport node and its controller. An ASON network element corresponds to a GMPLS transport node, and ASON control components correspond to a GMPLS controller.

GMPLS uses the term TE link (traffic engineering link) as a logical construct that groups physical resources for routing and path computation. ASON calls this an SNPP link (subnetwork point pool link). A GMPLS LSP (Label Switched Path) is an actual connection through the network; ASON calls this a network connection. A GMPLS layer (a set of resources of the same type) corresponds to an ASON layer network.
sections.eli5: In GMPLS, the router and its brain are called an LSR. In ASON, they are called a network element and control components. When one group talks about a TE link, the other calls it an SNPP link.

sections.title: Data Plane Resources and Capabilities
sections.content:
GMPLS defines data links as the physical or virtual connections between transport nodes. ASON calls these links in the context of subnetwork architecture. GMPLS distinguishes unidirectional (one-way) and bidirectional data links; ASON uses the same distinction. A link interface in GMPLS (which represents switching, termination, or adaptation capability) maps to ASON trail termination and adaptation functions.

GMPLS defines three switching capabilities: (1) switching (routing between resources in the same layer), (2) termination (ending a connection at a node), and (3) adaptation (using a connection in one layer as a link for another layer). ASON represents the same capabilities as properties of link ends, and calls them switching, termination, and adaptation properties.

GMPLS defines resource types by data encoding and switching granularity (PSC1, VC-12, Lambda 10G, etc.). ASON defines client characteristic information (CI)** as the payload type a resource can carry, which is essentially the same concept.
sections.eli5: Both systems talk about ports, links between ports, and what each port can do (switch, terminate, or adapt traffic). The words are different but the ideas are the same.

sections.title: Advanced Concepts: Hierarchies and Bundles
sections.content:
GMPLS defines a hierarchical LSP (H-LSP) as an LSP in one layer that becomes a link for another layer. ASON calls this a trail. GMPLS defines a Forwarding Adjacency (FA) as a TE link that does not require direct routing adjacency between controllers; ASON's equivalent is a trail advertised as a link. GMPLS defines a TE bundle as a group of parallel component links with similar properties, advertised as one TE link. ASON represents this as multiple SNPs and SNPP links with shared properties.

Both systems define TE domains (GMPLS) and layer networks (ASON) as regions with full visibility of TE information. Both support multi-layer integration: vertical integration (mechanisms spanning multiple layers) and horizontal integration (mechanisms spanning multiple domains). The detailed correspondence allows for precise mapping of complex scenarios like multi-domain optical networks.
sections.eli5: When you have many links in parallel, you can treat them as one big link. When a path becomes a link, it can carry traffic for another type of network. Both systems have these ideas but call them by different names.

sections.title: Application and Guidance
sections.content:
This lexicography is designed to help two communities work together. An ASON engineer reading a GMPLS specification can use this document to translate unfamiliar terminology into ASON concepts. An IETF engineer can understand how GMPLS applies to ASON requirements and architecture. For example, if a service provider wants to implement end-to-end protection using GMPLS, they can consult GMPLS protection RFCs and use this lexicography to map the design into their ASON infrastructure.

The document is not a substitute for the primary standards. For definitive GMPLS definitions, one must read RFC 3945 and the other GMPLS specifications. This lexicography is a companion that explains how GMPLS concepts fit into the ASON world. It also notes important limitations: GMPLS applies to many more data plane technologies than just ASON optical networks, so the mappings here are specific to the optical/ASON context.
sections.eli5: Use this to read GMPLS documents and translate them into ASON language, or vice versa. It helps the two communities understand each other's designs and specifications.
